| [NOTE-037](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-037.md) v2 | Debreu 1952, a social equilibrium existence theorem | Debreu proves existence of an equilibrium for an "abstract economy" (generalized game), in which each agent's feasible set A_ι(ā_ι) depends on the others' actions. The conditions: each action set 𝔄_ι is a contractible polyhedron; A_ι has a closed graph with non-empty compact values; f_ι is continuous on the graph into the extended reals; the value function φ_ι(ā_ι) = max f_ι is continuous; and each best-response set M_ā_ι is contractible. The proof applies the Eilenberg–Montgomery/Begle fixed-point theorem to the product best-response map. A Remark replaces the joint continuity of φ_ι with continuity (lower hemicontinuity) of A_ι plus a compact graph. A Corollary gives a saddle-point theorem that contains Kakutani's and von Neumann's. | Read |
| [NOTE-395](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-395.md) | Hindriks & Guala — Institutions, rules, and equilibria | Institutions are correlated equilibria of coordination games with several equilibria, represented by the players as rules. Searle's constitutive rules are derived from a regulative rule by coining a term that splits it into a base rule and a status rule; the term is conservative and eliminable, so constitutive rules add a name and cognitive economy, not a new kind of fact. The derivation is shown for one toy institution and asserted in general. The reply adds that normativity needs no constitutive rules, because a right is a bundle of other people's regulative obligations. | Read |
| [NOTE-404](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-404.md) | The Logic of Animal Conflict | Five strategies for contests with dangerous weapons, simulated 2,000 times per pairing with payoffs +60 win, −100 serious injury, −2 per scratch, up to +20 for brevity. | [NOTE-408](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-408.md) | Curry 2016, morality as cooperation: a problem-centred approach | The founding statement of morality-as-cooperation. | [NOTE-409](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-409.md) | Five Rules for the Evolution of Cooperation | A four-page review. | [NOTE-411](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-411.md) | The Evolution of Cooperation | TIT FOR TAT won Axelrod's two tournaments (14 entries plus random, 200 moves; 62 entries, expected 200 moves) and went to fixation in an ecological replay. Against it, only ALL D or alternation need be checked, so no strategy does better iff w ≥ (T−R)/(T−P) and w ≥ (T−R)/(R−S). ALL D is stable for all w; kinship or a cluster with enough in-cluster interactions lets reciprocity in, and a nice stable strategy resists clusters. ALL C ties with TIT FOR TAT, so stability is neutral, not strict. | Read |
| [NOTE-443](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-443.md) | Précis of Breakdown of Will | Hyperbolic discounting makes preference reverse with delay alone, so a person is a population of interests that forestall one another. | [NOTE-717](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-717.md) | Kamenica & Gentzkow — Bayesian Persuasion | With a common prior and a sender who commits to a signal the receiver sees, any distribution of posteriors whose mean is the prior can be induced, so the sender's best value is the concave closure of its posterior-value function at the prior (Corollary 2). | [NOTE-795](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-795.md) | Handfield et al. — Cooperative Dilemmas in Rational Debate | Two debaters move through a Betz-style space of truth assignments, each moving minimally when refuted, with payoff u = w·v − d (true beliefs against changes of mind). At moderate truth weights the truth-optimal equilibrium is asymmetric: one debater argues boldly and the other free-rides with a compromise strategy, a snowdrift dilemma. At low weights, or with error, both exit. In a narrow borderline region of mixed equilibria, raising the weight on truth lowers collective accuracy. A two-person model, n = 3 propositions, and every result is numerical. | Read |
| [NOTE-1033](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1033.md) | Kleinberg and Raghavan — Algorithmic monoculture and social welfare | Two firms each hire the best available candidate by either a private noisy ranking or one shared algorithmic ranking. If, at equal accuracy, a second mover prefers an independent ranking (preference for the first position) and is better off after a less accurate competitor (preference for weaker competition), then for every human accuracy there is a more accurate algorithm that both firms strictly prefer to use, yet both are worse off, and so is welfare, than if neither used it. The Mallows model meets the conditions for every candidate distribution; Gaussian and Laplacian random utility models meet them for three candidates; Plackett–Luce never does. | Read |
| [NOTE-1034](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1034.md) | Bergemann and Morris — Information design, a unified perspective | A designer who can commit to how players are informed, but not to what they do, can attain exactly the Bayes correlated equilibria: joint distributions of states and actions in which no player, told his recommended action, wants to deviate. The set is a polytope given by linear obedience constraints, so information design is a linear program over it. Read literally there is a designer; read metaphorically the set bounds what any information structure could produce. More prior information shrinks the set. Public signals serve a designer who wants correlated actions, private ones the reverse. Its two-firm example with strategic substitutes misstates the optimal rule for the parameters it assumes. | Read |
| [NOTE-1116](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1116.md) | Flows and Decompositions of Games: Harmonic and Potential Games | A finite game is read as a flow, the unilateral payoff differences on the graph of strategy profiles, and the Helmholtz decomposition of that flow splits the game uniquely into potential, harmonic and nonstrategic parts. | [NOTE-1132](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1132.md) | Soma et al. — The hive mind is a single reinforcement learning agent | A short theoretical paper with simulations. In an infinite, well-mixed population, imitation of success has the expected update of Cross Learning, and the weighted voter model of the honey-bee waggle dance that of Maynard-Cross Learning, the Maynard-Smith replicator dynamic. | [NOTE-1139](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1139.md) | Miller, Resnick and Zeckhauser — Eliciting informative feedback: the peer-prediction method | A mechanism-design paper with proofs and a worked example. A center with no ground truth pays each rater a strictly proper scoring rule applied to the posterior over a reference rater's report implied by her own report. Truth-telling is a strict Nash equilibrium, payments can be scaled to buy effort and balanced among raters, and coarse reports can be elicited for two types. Uninformative equilibria remain, and collusion, risk aversion, unelicited private signals and trust in the center are left as limits. | Read |
| [NOTE-1140](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1140.md) | Kaisers & Tuyls — Frequency adjusted multi-agent Q-learning | A short algorithmic paper with plotted experiments. The selection–mutation model of Boltzmann Q-learning (Tuyls et al. 2003, 2005) assumes every Q-value changes at rate α; in Q-learning only the chosen action's does, so its expected change carries a factor x_i, and Q-learning departs from the model depending on initialization. A frequency-adjusted update removes the factor and matches the model. Three 2×2 games, one temperature, no quantitative measure of fit. | Read |
| [NOTE-1141](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1141.md) | Son et al. — QTRAN: learning to factorize with transformation | Defines Individual-Global-Max (IGM): per-agent values factorise a joint value when the profile of individual argmaxes is the joint argmax. Additivity and monotonicity are sufficient conditions; QTRAN trains the sum of individual values plus a state value to equal the joint value at the greedy profile and bound it elsewhere, which is sufficient and, up to rescaling, necessary. Every single-state matrix game satisfies IGM; VDN and QMIX missed the optimum in 177 of 310 random 3×3 games. | Read |
| [NOTE-1142](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1142.md) | Hart & Mas-Colell — A simple adaptive procedure leading to correlated equilibrium | A theorem with a proof. Regret matching, switching from one's last action to each alternative with probability proportional to the positive regret for not having made that switch in the past, drives the empirical joint distribution of play almost surely to the set of correlated equilibria when every player uses it. Regrets vanish exactly when the empirical distribution approaches that set. A stylized variant is analysed by Blackwell approachability; the main procedure needs inertia and needs players to see one another's past play. | Read |
| [NOTE-1143](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1143.md) | Balduzzi et al. — Open-ended learning in symmetric zero-sum games | A framework paper with an algorithm and two small experiments. Symmetric zero-sum games between parametrized agents split into transitive and cyclic parts relative to a measure on agents. In a cyclic game an individual's performance is meaningless, so evaluation moves to populations: the value of the game between them, which is invariant to redundant members, and the convex hull of their evaluation rows. Training each supported agent on what it beats grows that hull. | Read |
| [NOTE-1144](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1144.md) | Sato & Crutchfield — Coupled replicator equations for the dynamics of learning in multiagent systems | A four-page letter. Two agents choose by softmax over reward memories that decay at rate α; with learning slow relative to play, each agent's choice distribution follows a replicator dynamic in the other's play plus α Σ_j x_j log(x_j/x_i), a pull towards uniform play. Without decay the system is conservative, Hamiltonian in zero-sum games; with decay it is dissipative. Rock–scissors–paper simulations show tori, Hamiltonian chaos, heteroclinic transients, limit cycles and chaotic attractors. Derivation plus numerics, no data. | Read |
| [NOTE-1146](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1146.md) | Czarnecki et al. — Real world games look like spinning tops | A hypothesis paper with theorems and sampled empirical games. Where players can signal n bits before the outcome is settled, every win–loss pattern on 2ⁿ strategies occurs, so cycles are astronomically long. Nash clustering layers any symmetric zero-sum game, and beating a whole cluster guarantees climbing. Sampled games show cluster size peaking at middling strength. The body says the geometry is not proved, the abstract says it is. Two of the smaller results have defective statements or proofs. | Read |
| [NOTE-1148](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1148.md) | Yang et al. — Mean field multi-agent reinforcement learning | An algorithms paper with a convergence proof and three experiments. Each agent's Q-function is approximated by its interaction with the mean action of its neighbours, which makes many-agent RL tractable for hundreds of homogeneous agents. Mean field Q-learning converges to a Nash Q-value under strong assumptions, learns Gaussian Squeeze with 500 and 1000 agents where baselines fail, matches MCMC on a 20 × 20 Ising model, and wins a 64-versus-64 battle game. | Read |
| [NOTE-1149](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1149.md) | Börgers & Sarin — Learning through reinforcement and replicator dynamics | A short theoretical paper. One Bush–Mosteller learner with payoffs in (0, 1), Cross's model, moves in expectation as a population under the discrete replicator step, and in the continuous-time limit follows the Taylor replicator dynamic at any finite time. For every learning speed, though, the discrete process is absorbed in a pure strategy profile with probability one. With negative payoffs a probability-matching force enters beside a replicator force. Proofs are by Euler's method and Norman's theorems on slow learning; the negative-payoff limit is stated with its proof omitted. | Read |
| [NOTE-1150](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1150.md) | Foerster et al. — Learning with opponent-learning awareness | A LOLA learner maximises its return after the opponent's anticipated naive gradient step and differentiates through that step, adding a second-order term to its gradient. Two exact-gradient LOLA learners reached tit-for-tat-like reciprocity in the memory-one iterated prisoner's dilemma where naive learners ended at mutual defection, and settled at the mixed equilibrium of iterated matching pennies where naive learners did not converge. A policy-gradient version cooperated in the Coin Game, less reliably with a learned model of the opponent. | Read |
| [NOTE-1151](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1151.md) | Leibo et al. — Multi-agent reinforcement learning in sequential social dilemmas | A descriptive simulation study. | [NOTE-1152](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1152.md) | Foerster et al. — Counterfactual multi-agent policy gradients | A centralised critic Q(s, τ, u) trains decentralised actors, and each agent's action is scored against the critic's average over its own alternatives under its own policy, the others' actions fixed. | [NOTE-1153](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1153.md) | Wolpert & Tumer — Optimal reward functions in distributed reinforcement learning | Members of a collective each run a reinforcement learner on a private utility, and the designer wants the world utility G maximised. | [NOTE-1154](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1154.md) | Rashid et al. — QMIX: monotonic value function factorisation | Per-agent values Q_a(τ^a, u^a) are combined into a joint Q_tot by a mixing network whose weights, generated from the state, are kept non-negative, so ∂Q_tot/∂Q_a ≥ 0. | [NOTE-1155](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1155.md) | Balduzzi et al. — Re-evaluating evaluation | A methods paper with two short applications. It reads evaluation data as antisymmetric matrices. As α grows its transitions become those of Markov-Conley chains, the sinks of the better-response graph, which the paper ties to chain components of the replicator flow. | [NOTE-1159](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1159.md) | Kwon and Perchet — Blackwell approachability with partial monitoring: optimal convergence rates | Approachability of a polytope (reduced to the negative orthant) under partial monitoring, where the decision maker sees only a random signal whose law is known, can be achieved at rate O(T^-1/3) in expected distance for general signals and O(T^-1/2) when the signal law does not depend on the decision. | [NOTE-1162](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1162.md) | Lattimore and Szepesvári — Cleaning up the neighborhood: a full classification for adversarial partial monitoring | Completes the classification of finite partial-monitoring games against oblivious adversaries to every game, degenerate and duplicate actions included: 0 with no neighbouring pair, Θ̃(√n) locally observable, Θ(n^2/3) globally but not locally observable, Ω(n) otherwise. The missing piece is NeighborhoodWatch2, which redistributes probability onto degenerate actions in proportion to the neighbours they lie between and has a high-probability √n bound. | [NOTE-1164](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1164.md) v2 | Bartók, Foster, Pál, Rakhlin and Szepesvári — Partial monitoring: classification, regret bounds and algorithms | For finite partial-monitoring games the minimax regret takes exactly four rates: 0 with one non-dominated action, Θ̃(√T) when every pair of neighbouring actions is locally observable, Θ(T^2/3) when the game is globally but not locally observable, and Θ(T) otherwise. The conditions are linear algebra on loss and signal matrices: a loss difference must lie in the span of the row spaces of the signal matrices of the actions allowed to estimate it. The stochastic classification covers every game; the adversarial one covers non-degenerate games only. | Read |
